courseDetails.name: Culture Wars: Introducing Culture and Social Justice
courseDetails.content: Struggles for social justice often make use of cultural symbols, artistic forms of expression and language as a tool of dissent. They thereby challenge hard-wired assumptions around the stability of cultures and call into question who belongs or is excluded from culture’s terrains. At the same time, these contestations take place in an increasingly polarised world wherein cultures are imagined as ideological battlegrounds and pitted against each other. Rather than debunking or defensively responding to what tend to be presented as 'culture wars', this module instead takes a closer and more in-depth look at the place of the arts and culture in struggles for social justice around the world.

courseDetails.name: Skills: Writing About Arts, Culture and Politics
courseDetails.content: In this course students will gain a firm foundation in the creation of text for different media and purposes. During the seminars a range styles of writing will be introduced and applied, with a particular focus on the basics of academic writing. Students will gain experience in providing editorial feedback on the texts of others as well as AI-generated texts. The foundations of academic writing, referencing, revision, peer review, the use of AI and other software tools will be discussed in class and practised in groups or on one's own. Students will work towards writing an opinion piece, among other pieces of writing.

courseDetails.name: Historicising the Global
courseDetails.content: This course offers students a historical perspective on some of the main themes and topics covered in the Global Arts, Culture and Politics programme. To do this the course traces and unsettles the emergence of ''The Global'' in relation to key artistic, cultural and historical developments of the past 500 years, from colonialism and capitalism to globalisation and the threat of climate change. This ''big picture'' approach aims to historicise contemporary global challenges and explore some of the different ways students might understand and address major societal issues through culture and the arts.The course begins from the premise that ''The Global'' is far from a neutral concept. The idea of The Globe is closely tied to histories of empire, resource extraction, economic development, mobility and migration, rights and law, scientific knowledge, and the movement of people around the planet – both forced and unforced. To help ground this approach we will explore the different ways ''The Global'' has been conceptualised from Amsterdam – a city that is deeply connected to histories of colonialism, slavery, capitalism and post-war globalisation. We will look at archives and other historic records to shed light on the social, intellectual, and aesthetic emergence of the globe over the past five centuries. At the same time, through course readings, seminar discussions and their own research, students will investigate alternative global histories and imaginaries drawn from varied cultural and artistic practices. Assignments focus on clarifying and unsettling the idea of "The Global" from different perspectives. Additional guidance in developing and writing the final essay will be provided in the concurrent course Skills: Writing About Arts, Culture and Politics.

courseDetails.name: Philosophy of Science and the Humanities
courseDetails.content: This course familiarises you with key modes of thought at the intersection of Science and the Humanities since the modern faculties were established in the early 19th century. The course introduces students to formative debates from which lasting frameworks of analysis emerged in the 20th century, with historical background provided in lecture. Each week focuses on a key moment in the formation of the sciences and humanities with particular attention to its epistemic impact on contemporary research cultures in the academy and the specialisation streams of Global Arts, Culture, and Politics.

courseDetails.name: Skills: Visual Literacy
courseDetails.entry: This course is only accessible to students of the Global Arts, Culture and Politics programme.
courseDetails.content: Art and museums play a prominent role in ongoing global debates about history and how history is (re)presented today. Visual literacy is essential to actively partake in global debates about history, inclusion, and representation. In museums, you will learn how to look at, describe and analyse works of art from different periods, how to formulate an argument based on your observations, and apply these analytical tools to non-art objects. In small groups and step by step, you will become better versed, confident, and skilled at discussing art and museum presentations in light of your own observations and views.

courseDetails.name: Writing Women into History: Introducing Curating the Past
courseDetails.content: In recent years, worldwide public debates about injustice and inequality have changed how we present and think about the past. Subsequently, a wide range of missing and underrepresented subjects and persons have been and are being written into history. New perspectives continuously allow for fresh insights, which require language changes. But what does it mean to revise history and to present a more inclusive version of the past? As an introduction to the major 'Curating the Past', this course uses the subject of women and gender inequality as an example to demonstrate the challenges and consequences of revisionist history. In a changing world rich with viewpoints, definitive answers are hard to come by, so you will learn methods and concrete instruments to approach topical questions. You will be actively engaged to rethink the past and the present, and you will position yourself within academic and public debates.

courseDetails.name: The Power of Persuasion I: Rhetoric in an Information Age
courseDetails.content: This course introduces the system of classical rhetoric through key works by Aristotle, Cicero, and Quintilian. Their theories shaped the European curriculum for centuries and were adapted from the Roman world (e.g. Julius Caesar) to the early modern period (e.g. Erasmus and Shakespeare).The course is structured around the five traditional tasks of the orator (officia oratoris). After a general introduction, each task is explored in a dedicated lecture. In the final part, we turn to two applications of rhetorical theory: identifying and characterising populist rhetoric and its appeal, and analysing visual communication and its persuasive force.Classical theory is consistently brought into dialogue with contemporary practice. We apply rhetorical concepts to modern speeches from diverse professions, cultures, and traditions, and to other forms of persuasive discourse, such as campaign videos, social media, and artworks. Students are invited to contribute their own examples, especially speeches and speakers overlooked in the classical canon.Throughout the course, students are challenged to think critically about how persuasive communication shapes opinions and behaviours, and to respond to such rhetoric in a reflective and responsible manner.

courseDetails.name: Cultural Sociology
courseDetails.content: This course introduces students to influential thinkers and key concepts in cultural sociology. It begins by examining the political, cultural, and economic conditions in Western Europe that gave rise to the discipline of sociology. This specific historical and geographical context has shaped the core assumptions and concepts of foundational sociological theories.In response, the course also explores the societal structures, forms of knowledge, and historical events that have been excluded from mainstream sociological texts—such as (Black) feminist thought, queer experiences, colonisation, and decolonisation.Although the sociological canon has long claimed universality, the course critically examines its Eurocentric foundations. This critique does not imply that the work of Western sociologists is without value. Rather, it underscores the importance of recognising the limitations of these theories and encourages openness to dialogue with alternative perspectives.Accordingly, the course also introduces students to the ongoing conversations among diverse sociologies, aiming to foster the development of a more inclusive, pluriversal sociology.

courseDetails.name: Skills: Digital Literacy & Archival Research
courseDetails.content: In this course, you will learn about organising digital and analogue information, through learning by doing. We will practice gathering and differentiating the information on the Internet, in the library and in the archive. We will combine reading on introductory theoretical reflections on digitisation and archiving, with critical understanding and training basic digital research skills. The class attends to reflexivity, ethics and the challenges of online research.

courseDetails.name: Fake News: Introducing The Human and AI
courseDetails.content: This course will focus on the societal implications of artificial intelligence (AI) in contemporary art, culture, and politics. In particular, we will study the role of generative AI tools, such as (Chat)GPT, Claude, Midjourney, and Faceswap, in today's society. How do these technologies work and how is their work perceived by the public? During the course, students will generate or react to AI-generated content in a short reflection and will try to train each other to effectively use AI-generated content in out-of-class groupwork. At the end of the course, students will understand major trends in generative AI, the political choices behind its creation and use, and have the foundations to critique the artistic, cultural, and political implications of generative AI.

courseDetails.name: Skills: Interviews & On-Site Research
courseDetails.content: In this course students learn about doing and using interviews and other on-site research methods, through learning by doing. Beyond theoretical introduction, the focus will be on understanding and training basic research skills. You will learn about different techniques and methods, but also prepare and conduct an interview in a small team, and make observations of your own. Attention will be devoted to reflexivity, ethics and the challenges of on-site (field) research.

courseDetails.name: Earth Politics and the Future of Life: Introducing Reimagining Sustainability
courseDetails.content: This course builds on Raymond William's thesis that the idea of nature contains an extraordinary amount of human history. This would mean that the current climate emergency is manmade, and thus an entirely political and ethical phenomenon of a planetary scale. To help ground this wide-ranging subject the course looks to biocentric, nonhegemonic understandings of nature, development, and sustainability. This approach brings together practical issues of environmental sustainability with urgent questions around climate justice, decoloniality, and the role of art in fostering more sustainable ways of living that would secure the future of life. We will look at key case studies from around the world and relate these to the politics and ethics of the climate emergency.

courseDetails.name: Global Politics and Power
courseDetails.content: It is not easy to understand global politics. It is a messy and confusing subject, covering a range of pressing topics (economics, security, climate change, justice, dependency, etc.) and a multitude of actors and relations that are interacting and changing. To understand what is changing and why, should we for instance look at what the United Nations General Assembly decides, or rather pay attention to the World Economic Forum (Davos)? Why does violence remain widespread, despite the fact that over the past century numerous rules and institutions have been set up to prevent violence? Is the rise of China empowering the Global South or could it be a new imperial power? And have we currently entered an era of de-globalisation, and what does this imply for states, enterprises and citizens?How we look at these and other visible and invisible global shifts partly depends on how we understand what power is and how it works. In this course we will look at the ways in which global politics have changed, and how this is shaped by power as well as ideas, ideologies and institutions across scales (global, national and local). We will read and discuss concepts and theories developed by different influential scholars from around the globe. While we will see that some long-standing ideas still influence current thinking and politics, we will also critically review common views on politics and power, and learn how to theorise.

courseDetails.name: Philosophy of Art & Culture
courseDetails.content: This course familiarises you with key modes of philosophical thought at the intersection of art and culture. On the one hand, philosophical concepts and reflection play a part in making art and culture what they are; on the other, artworks and other cultural productions engage in philosophical questioning. What trajectories of making, doing, thinking, feeling, perceiving, and relating make up this interplay between philosophy, culture and art? What can we make of aspects of participation, performance, and value? And how do dimensions of race, gender, class, sexuality, coloniality, and the global come in? We will examine classical as well as contemporary readings and artworks in multiple cultural traditions.

courseDetails.name: The Power of Persuasion II: Argumentation in an Information Age
courseDetails.content: This course introduces students to the analysis and evaluation of persuasive discourse, with a focus on argumentation. Students learn to look beyond surface-level rhetoric and examine the argumentative backbone of persuasive texts: how claims are supported, how reasoning can go wrong, and what makes an argument genuinely strong rather than merely persuasive. The course moves from theoretical foundations to analytical skills, building competence and critical awareness in parallel.The course is organised into three blocks, each roughly corresponding to the stages of argument-checking: argument detection and mapping, argument type identification, and argumentation assessment. Topics and sub-topics include:1. Argument detection and mappingFinding argumentative elements in real-world persuasive texts. Reconstructing standpoints and reasons. Dealing with implicit, incomplete, and ambiguous argumentation. Identifying argumentation structures.2. Argument type identificationExploring the characteristics of various argument types within the framework of the Periodic Table of Arguments. Identifying argument types in persuasive discourse.3. Argumentation assessmentAssessing the quality of arguments by applying normative criteria systematically. Distinguishing strong arguments from fallacies.

courseDetails.name: Life of an Object
courseDetails.content: The seminar course Life of an Object is taught parallel with the lecture series Revisionist Histories and aims to deepen your understanding of the ways in which histories are subject to change. The course is object-based and interdisciplinary, with art history at its core. We will meet twice a week in a seminar or museum setting. During our sessions you are invited to actively engage with the making, movement, and meaning of specific objects. You will further train yourself in academic research and writing. Making optimal use of local museum collections, you will experience firsthand what it means to (re)write overlooked subjects into history, to challenge established narratives. Throughout the course we ask ourselves: what does it mean to curate the past?

courseDetails.name: Revisionist Histories
courseDetails.content: History, by definition, is ever-changing. What is emphasised in which history books? And why are historical narratives subject to perpetual change? Motivated by global debates and challenges, 'Revisionist Histories' aims to challenge the notion of a canon. It does so with an object-based approach, considering the making, movement, and meaning of things. This lecture series demonstrates the potential of the study of objects in the presentation of a more inclusive and more nuanced version of the past and how such pasts resonate in the present. Together with the seminar course 'Life of an Object,' taught parallel to this course, this class equips you with a solid foundation for discussing ideas about the material, historical and social contexts of objects. It will encourage you to engage critically with the challenges of our time.

courseDetails.name: Mapping World Views
courseDetails.content: Maps present the world in a single glance. Or so it seems. Maps are fascinating documents conveying as well as shaping past, current, and future views on the globe and its parts. In this course students learn to find maps and to critically analyse and interpret their contents and messages. What does it mean when a map is considered to be accurate or objective? Or are maps always distorted and subjective? Hence, what is the value of cartographic data for studying and practising arts, culture and politics? Through searching for (old) maps in analogue and digital map collections, analysing and interpreting their forms, components and contents, and drawing new maps, the students of this course will rethink their worlds and environments from multiple perspectives.

courseDetails.name: The Archival Revolution: Applying Digital Tools to Render the Invisible Visible
courseDetails.content: This course invites students into the dynamic field of archival research, highlighting its potential and limits in revealing untold stories of historically marginalised experiences with a focus on colonial, racial and gendered dynamics of power and resistance. The course offers an introduction to the history of archives, how archives are organised and accessed, methods for conducting critical archival research, methods and frameworks to examine and engage with archival records and historical documents critically, and how digital technologies and tools are reshaping and changing how archival research takes place and what we can do with records. Students will engage with (innovative, critical) analog and online archiving and research tools together with automated transcription platforms. With these critical and advanced methods, students will be confronted with the challenges posed by the reduced perspective of an archive(s) or collection, created by the historically dominant lens of patriarchal, colonial relations. Through a blend of theoretical learning and practical application, this course aims to equip students with a foundational understanding of archival research in the context of promoting inclusivity in historical representations and narratives.

courseDetails.name: Visual Art and Power
courseDetails.content: The production and possession of visual art has long been used as a means to assert power. At the same time, the potency of art has frequently been deployed by those who seek to challenge and subvert existing power structures. There are numerous examples of talented artists around the world who, for centuries, have used art to persuasively give power it's visual form. There are also the individuals and institutions who are able to use their power to obtain and retain art, in turn enhancing their status further. This course will start by presenting students with some inspiring case studies. These will provide students with an understanding of the co-dependent relationship between art and power as it relates to the themes of religion, gender, rebellion, money and restitution.The second part of the course will apply students' knowledge of the relationship between art and power to global and local issues that matter to the people of Amsterdam. As Amsterdam protests in recent years have shown – Black Lives Matter, the Climate March, Pro-Palestine protests, the Feminist March, Pride – Amsterdam is an important site for global issues. Students will be asked to identify a power imbalance they view as urgent, identify an artist with a relevant body of work, and propose how the city of Amsterdam can use art to enact meaningful change. Amsterdam thus provides a tangible location in which art can be used to do something about the global and local issues that its inhabitants care about. An external jury, which will include representatives from the Amsterdam Municipality, will attend and judge the final presentation of students' ideas.

courseDetails.name: Theatre and the Construction of Society
courseDetails.content: Theatre has always been Europe's platform to present, test, and reimagine different versions of Europe's histories, societies, and futures. Greek tragedies underpinned how democracy formed in ancient Athens. Early-modern theatres critiqued the present and imagined future of monarchies. The nineteenth century saw theatre as representing and creating a nation. The post-World War II international festivals performed international unity and collaborations. Today, from the mainstream stages through disability-led theatres, migrant theatre, and the Covid-19-inspired digital theatre works, theatre continues to be a place where Europe, nations, and changes are reimagined, pre-rehearsed, and re-performed.In this course, students will explore how theatre is a place of rehearsing, imagining and constructing societies from ancient ideas on democracy to contemporary moments in Europe. Through diverse case studies from Greece, Spain, Netherlands, Poland, and contemporary multilingual Europe, the classes will examine how individual societies have created their own ideas and practices of theatre and its socio-political role, and how they have developed their own structures for theatre to happen.

courseDetails.name: The Power of the Written Word
courseDetails.content: In the early modern period, just as today, media played a fundamental role in the global dissemination of knowledge, shaping societies and affecting various groups in diverse ways. This course delves into the intricate dynamics of historical media, examining not only their tangible formats but also their substantive content. By scrutinising publications, intermediaries, audiences, and the flow of knowledge and information across geographical, religious, and social divides, we aim to unravel the multifaceted impact and power of media throughout history. From texts and manuscripts to early printed materials and beyond, we explore how media have both empowered and marginalised different communities, illuminating the complex interplay between communication technologies and societal structures. Join us on a journey through time to uncover the profound significance of media in shaping the early modern world and its enduring relevance in contemporary society.

courseDetails.name: GACP Thesis Research Lab
courseDetails.content: The Thesis is the final assessment of the GACP Programme. It consists of two components: a Research Lab (6EC), and the Thesis itself (12EC).Students plan, develop and write their thesis in the second semester of the third year. In Block 4 (Feb-March) they are guided by a lecturer in thematic Research Labs organised around key themes in Global Arts, Culture and Politics. Students respond to these themes with their own research project, developed in dialogue with the Thesis Group leader and peers. The Research Labs offer space to explore the overarching theme, but also offer more general guidance on the design and development of a research project, from formulating research questions to choosing an appropriate methodology and analysing research “data” (broadly defined). The Lab concludes with a Final Research Proposal including a clear question (or set of questions), a brief state-of-the-art (lit review), a description of the original research to be conducted (methods and theoretical framing), a provisional overview of chapters, and a bibliography of key sources and references. The Proposal should be approved by the Thesis Group leader before any primary research begins.In Blocks 5 and 6 students undertake independent research under the supervision of their Thesis Group leader. This will include two individual meetings to monitor progress, offer guidance on literature, methods, structure and theory, and provide feedback on draft chapters. Students will also benefit from peer feedback in writing workshops, thesis surgeries and a Work-in-Progress symposium bringing together the different Thesis Groups. The Final Thesis of between 9,000 and 12,000 words (excluding annotations, footnotes, bibliography, captions etc.) must be submitted by the end of Block 6. No supervision is possible after June under any circumstances.

progression: The 60 EC first year includes 30 EC each semester. The English diagnostic test and tutoring are zero-credit requirements. The student completes the first year and obtains positive binding study advice before entering the post-propaedeutic curriculum.

The adopted Appendix and dated catalogue replace the generic overview’s second-year common subjects with Philosophy of Art & Culture and The Power of Persuasion II. The seven Curating the Past units total 48 EC. Life of an Object runs alongside Revisionist Histories. The first semester has 18 major EC plus 12 common EC; the second has 30 major EC. The standard track uses no double-degree substitutions.

The final-year example can place 30 open elective EC in the first semester and 12 in block 4 with the 6 EC research lab. The lab ends with a proposal and approval before primary research; blocks 5 and 6 are independent research and writing for the 12 EC thesis. The programme counts the lab and thesis once each.
